H1_traffic.hypothesis: H1: Delivery duration differs significantly across traffic densities
H1_traffic.interpretation: Delivery duration exhibits a statistically significant difference across traffic conditions (Kruskal-Wallis H=8261.55, p < 0.001; eta-squared=0.183). Jam traffic conditions add an average of 9.9 minutes compared to Low traffic, representing a large effect size (Cohen's d=1.16).

H2_weather.hypothesis: H2: Delivery duration differs across weather conditions
H2_weather.interpretation: Weather conditions have a statistically significant relationship with delivery duration (Kruskal-Wallis H=2784.72, p < 0.001). Adverse weather such as Fog, Stormy, and Sandstorms consistently increases delivery duration compared to Sunny conditions (by ~6.7 minutes).

H3_peak_hours.hypothesis: H3: Peak hours exhibit longer delivery durations than non-peak hours
H3_peak_hours.interpretation: Peak hours (Lunch and Dinner) show a statistically significant increase in delivery time (mean difference = 4.93 mins, 95% CI [4.76, 5.10], p < 0.001). While statistically significant due to large sample size (N=45,584), the practical effect size is modest (Cohen's d=0.54), confirming that traffic and distance remain the dominant drivers of total variance.

H4_vehicle_type.hypothesis: H4: Delivery duration differs across vehicle types
H4_vehicle_type.interpretation: Vehicle types show a statistically significant difference (Kruskal-Wallis H=1080.53, p < 0.05). Bicycles exhibit slightly different operational constraints compared to motorized vehicles.

H5_satisfaction.hypothesis: H5: Delayed deliveries are associated with lower customer satisfaction ratings
H5_satisfaction.decision: Fail to Reject H0 (No Significant Linear Association)
H5_satisfaction.interpretation: In the FoodHub dataset (N=1162 rated orders), the rank correlation between delivery time and customer rating is weak (Spearman rho = 0.001, p = 0.981). Dissatisfied customers (rating <= 3) had an average delivery time of 24.6 mins compared to 24.1 mins for satisfied customers (rating >= 4). Importantly, 38.78% of orders had 'Not given' ratings. This empirical finding demonstrates that satisfaction in instant food delivery is multi-factorial (food quality, order accuracy, packaging temperature) and cannot be accurately predicted solely from transit duration.
